It includes shallow edges and deeper areas, making it easy for amphibians to move in and out. The pond will support wildlife such as frogs, newts, dragonflies and damselflies.; Planting for wildlife; The pond has been planted with a range of native species to support insects and aquatic life. These include:; Myosotis scorpioides (Water forget-me-not); Juncus effusus (Common rush); Veronica beccabunga (Brooklime); Nymphaea alba (White waterlily); Persicaria amphibia (Amphibious bistort); Wildflower areas and bee habitats; Excavated soil was separated into topsoil and London clay sub soil to create mounds of diverse substrates for different flowering plants. Thanet sand was used to add a soft, low nutrient medium to attract different plants and for mining bees to nest in. The mounds are planted with native wildflowers including:; Achillea millefolium (Yarrow); Centaurea nigra (Common knapweed); Prunella vulgaris (Selfheal); Cynosurus cristatus (Crested dogstail); Leucanthemum vulgare (Oxeye daisy); Additional habitats; Around the pond, you can find a range of features designed to help wildlife:; dead branches for insects and perching birds; a small dead hedge of twigs for fungi, beetles and wood mice; a mini hibernaculum for newts and slow worms; a clay wall for mason and flower bees to nest in, covered by a small green roof; a low, recycled rubble wall with clay mortar (for spiders and mason bees); bee towers drilled with “beetle” holes for bees to nest in; We have already recorded mallard ducks, water boatmen, damselflies, broad bodied chasers, mining bees and mason bees using the site.; Location; location; Address; Downhills Park Road and Boundary Road London N22 6AD United Kingdom ; Opening times; Open 24 hours a day.; Accessibility; All Haringey park are accessible to wheelchair users.; You must have JavaScript enabled to use this form.; Was this page useful? ; Leave this field empty ; Help us improve haringey.gov.uk; To help us improve this website, we'd like to know more about your visit today.; Feedback; Give us feedback on this page Opens in new window ; Sory there is a problem; Unfortunately we are currently having issues connecting to our feedback service. Its rich history dates back to the early 11th century. ; Facilities and things to do and see; Facilities; Bruce Castle Park has:; basketball courts; a café – for café information visit the Pavillion Cafe website ; a multi-use games area; a paddling pool – for opening times please see our paddling pool page ; a picnic area; a playground; table tennis table; tennis courts – book a court on the Bruce Castle tennis website ; toilets – in the museum; Tree trail; The museum and parks service produced a tree trail for the park. It details an exciting trail for children to follow.; Download a copy and start exploring:; tree trail ( pdf , 3 page(s) , 808.15 KB ) ; tree identification information ( pdf , 2 page(s) , 516.83 KB ) ; Oak tree; A magnificent ancient oak tree dominates the northern side of the park. It's believed to be about 500 years old and came runner up in the Woodland Trust’s Tree of the Year award for England in 2018. ; Holocaust Memorial Garden; The park is home to a Holocaust Memorial Garden, honouring those killed by Nazis in the second world war.; Get involved; The park has a volunteer group called a Friends group.; To find out more about the group and get involved, see our list of Friends of Parks groups .; Park management; To find out how the park is managed see our park management reports page .; Green Flag Award; First awarded the prestigious Green Flag Award in 2003, Bruce Castle Park has kept it ever since.; To ask for a copy of the Green Flag report see our parks report page .; History; The park was created from the remains of the ancient Bruce Castle family estate, bought by the council in 1892.; Bruce Castle Museum and Archive, located in the park, is a Grade I listed 16th century manor house. It houses the Haringey’s local history collections and archives and has been open since 1906. See how many you can spot. ; Get involved; The Wood has an information group of volunteers called Friends of Coldfall Wood. They share a common interest in protecting and enhancing the wood. ; To find out more about the group and get involved, see our list of Friends of Parks groups .; Wood management ; To find out how the park is managed see our park management reports page .; Sustainable woodland management ; We have achieved forest certification at Coldfall Wood under the UK Woodland Assurance Standard (UKWAS). ; UKWAS sets out management standards for woodland owners and managers and is accredited by the Forest Stewardship Council.; Coppicing ; The wood has historically been managed through coppicing. This is where trees are cut down at the base. New growth then comes from the stump and cut trees are left to naturally decay.; The dead wood contributes to a healthy woodland as it makes a great home for beetles and other insects and fungi. These provide food for woodland creatures like birds and hedgehogs. ; Coppicing allows in light for wildflowers and other plants attracting butterflies and other animals. 150 additional plant species were recorded in Coldfall Wood since November 2006. ; Report a problem; Report a park issue on our report a problem page .; Location; location; Address; Creighton Avenue London N10 1HU United Kingdom ; Opening times; Open 24 hours a day.; Accessibility; The only accessible entrances are:; Creighton Avenue West ; Creighton Avenue East ; You must have JavaScript enabled to use this form.; Was this page useful? ; Leave this field empty ; Help us improve haringey.gov.uk; To help us improve this website, we'd like to know more about your visit today.; Feedback; Give us feedback on this page Opens in new window ; Sory there is a problem; Unfortunately we are currently having issues connecting to our feedback service.
